title: Emotional development in babies

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The helpless, seemingly unaware infant staring up at you from a crib has a lot more going on inside her head than you ever imagined. New research is leading pediatricians and child psychologists to rethink long-held beliefs about the emotional and intellectual abilities of even very young babies. In 1890, psychologist William James famously described an infant's view of the world as 'one great blooming, buzzing confusion.' It was a notion that held for nearly a century: infants were simple-minded creatures who merely copied those around them and understood only the most basic emotions - happiness, sadness, anger. Science is now providing a much different picture of what goes on inside their hearts and heads. Long before they form their first words, babies are already mastering complex emotions jealousy, empathy, frustration that were once thought to be learned when they became toddlers (18 months to 3 years old).

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Armed with this new information, pediatricians are starting to alter the way they evaluate their youngest patients. In addition to tracking physical development, they are now focusing much more deeply on emotional advancement. The research shows how important emotional development is to a child's well-being. A baby who does not reach certain key early 'emotional milestones' may have trouble learning to speak and read and, later, performing academically. By reading emotional responses, physicians have begun to discover ways to tell if a baby as young as 3 months is showing early signs of possible psychological problems or learning disabilities. 'Instead of just asking parents if their babies are crawling or sitting, we are asking, do they point to things? When they see a new person, how do they react?' says Dr. Chet Johnson, of the American Academy of Pediatrics. 'How children do on social, emotional and language skills is a better predictor of success in adulthood than motor skills are.'

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: One of the earliest emotions that even newborn babies display is empathy. If a newborn is placed next to another crying infant, chances are both babies will soon be crying. 'People have always known that babies cry when they hear other babies cry,' says Martin Hoffman, a psychology professor at New York University. 'The question was, why are they crying?' Does it mean that the baby is truly concerned for his fellow human, or just annoyed by the noise? A recent study, which built on Hoffman's own work, has largely answered the question. Researchers played tapes for infants of other babies crying. As predicted, the tears began flowing. However, when researchers played recordings of their own cries to the babies, they rarely began crying themselves. The verdict: 'There is some basic empathy in place, right from birth,' Hoffman says. The intensity of the emotion tends to fade over time. Babies older than 6 months no longer cry but grimace at the discomfort of others. By 13 to 15 months, babies tend to take control of the situation they will try to comfort a crying playmate.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Part of that empathy may come from another early-baby skill that is now better understood – the ability to interpret emotions from the facial expressions of the people around them. 'Most textbooks still say that babies younger than 6 months do not recognize emotions,' says Diane Montague, assistant professor of psychology at LaSalle University. To put that belief to the test, Montague came up with a twist on every infant's favorite game, peek-a-boo, and recruited dozens of 4-month-olds to play. She began by peeking around a cloth with a big smile on her face. Predictably, the babies were delighted, and stared at her intently, the time-tested way to tell if a baby is interested. On the fourth peek, though, Montague emerged with a sad look on her face. This time, the response was much different. 'They not only looked away,' she says, 'but they wouldn't look back even when I began smiling again.' Refusing to make eye contact is a classic baby sign of distress. An angry face got their attention again, but their faces showed no pleasure. 'I realize it is speculative but I think it shows that babies younger than 6 months find meaning in expressions.'

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: When infants are near their first birthdays, they become increasingly adept social learners. They begin to infer what others are thinking by following the gaze of those around them. 'By understanding where others' eyes look, babies come to understand others' minds,' says Andrew Meltzoff, a professor of psychology at the University of Washington who has studied the 'gaze following' of thousands of babies. 'You can tell a lot about people, what they are interested in and what they intend to do next, by watching their eyes. It appears that even babies know that.' Meltzoff and colleague Rechele Brooks have found that this skill first appears at 10 to 11 months, and is not only an important marker of a baby's emotional and social growth, but can predict later language development. In Meltzoff and Brooks's study, babies who were not proficient at gaze following by their first birthday had fewer advanced language skills when they were 2 years old.
